CEST-detectable metabolite candidates: pancreas

1 of 5 candidates clear the simulated with-vs-without contrast threshold (0.5%) at some field strength, by chemical exchange (downfield, +ppm) or by the relayed NOE (upfield, −ppm). 1 fall below it; 3 are unknown because no group had a verified reference rate, so nothing could be simulated. The threshold applies to our own simulation, never to a literature MTRasym.

Mobile protein/peptide amide pool — CEST: ✓ detectable (rNOE)

Concentration: 30.00 mM typical (~10-100 mM (estimated, order-of-magnitude, no pancreas-specific value found))

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: ESTIMATE, not a measured value. No pancreas-specific amide-pool mM figure was found in the accessed literature. The value is inferred from tissue composition: pancreas is ~70-80% water with ~10-20% (w/w) total protein, comparable to other protein-dense parenchyma where APT is routinely imaged. At ~15% protein and ~72 g/mol per backbone amide residue, 150 mg protein/g tissue / (0.8 g tissue / g water) ~ 188 mg protein/g water ~ 2.6 mM backbone amide. The mobile (non-immobile) fraction is only a subset, but side-chain amides/amine groups add to the 3.5 ppm pool, so tens of mM is a reasonable order-of-magnitude. Flagged as a rough estimate.

Derivation stepValueSource
Pancreas water fraction ~75-80% by weight.~0.78 g water / g tissueassumption
Pancreas total protein ~10-20% by weight; mid estimate used.~150 mg protein / g tissueassumption
Convert protein mass to backbone amide residues: 100 mg protein = 15.6 mmol residues at 72 g/mol per amide (1 residue per residue, 1 NH each).1.39 mmol amide residues / g tissuecalculation: 150 mg / 72 g/mol = 2.08 mmol residues/g tissue
Normalize to water: 2.08 mmol / 0.78 g water = 2.7 mM backbone amide (this is the lower bound for the amide backbone alone).~2.7 mM backbone amidecalculation
Side-chain amide/amine groups (Asn, Gln) and mobile peptides add further exchangeable protons at ~3.5 ppm, so the practical APT pool is higher than the backbone-only lower bound; report a representative tens-of-mM figure.~30 mM representativeassumption: order-of-magnitude analogy to protein-dense parenchyma APT signal (PMID 27272542, 24474497)

Exchangeable protons: backbone amide N-H (1H, +3.50 ppm, intermediate (slow-ish), classic APT amide exchange, exchangeable); side-chain hydroxyl OH (Ser/Thr/Tyr) (1H, +1.00 ppm, fast, free -OH often merges into water tail exchange, exchangeable); aliphatic C-H (rNOE) (11H, -3.50 ppm, rNOE (dipolar, relayed) exchange, not exchangeable)

Reference database (biofluid — for comparison, not a tissue value): TISSUE — no curated pancreas concentration found in BioNumbers for this metabolite; the tissue number in this report is therefore not reference-grounded

Recommended field strength(s): 1.5 T, 3 T, 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: fragile

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (aliphatic C-H (rNOE) [rnoe]: concentration 10-100 mM, kex fixed at 5 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown)) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.11-1.08%, 1.5 T: 0.23-2.26%, 3 T: 0.31-3.00%, 5 T: 0.42-4.09%, 7 T: 0.48-4.65%. Threshold 0.5%. Only the point estimate clears the threshold; the low corner does not.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • rNOE (-3.5 ppm) sits ON the semisolid MT wing (-2.4 ppm) at all fields: separation 23-328 Hz vs ~16 kHz combined MT linewidth, so the rNOE dip cannot be isolated from MT by frequency - classic APT/rNOE/MT confusion, but the dip amplitude is still detectable.
  • Amide (+3.5 ppm) overlaps the L-glutamine amide (+3.5 ppm) at 0 Hz - see glutamine verdict; here one combined APT pool. Amide vs hydroxyl: 2.5 ppm apart, resolved at >=1.5T. rNOE vs amide 7 ppm apart, no collision. Dominant concern is MT background under rNOE, not metabolite-vs-metabolite blur.

Direct water saturation: Swept B1 0.25-0.5 µT. Direct-sat bandwidth 10.6 Hz (0.25 µT) at 0.5-3T, 21.3 Hz (0.5 µT) at 5-7T. rNOE and amide offsets 234-328 Hz from water - 10-15x the direct-sat band, no masking. Hydroxyl (+1 ppm) is 68-211 Hz from water at 1.5-7T (outside band), but at 0.5T only ~17.5 Hz, at the edge of the 10.6 Hz band, so the 0.5T hydroxyl CEST (0.045%) is partly masked by direct saturation - consistent with its very low contrast.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat:

  • All three kex BORROWED, not pancreas-specific: amide 65.5 s−1 is the median of 2 human-in-vivo (brain) values with a 15-158 s−1 spread; hydroxyl 600 s−1 is a single myo-inositol/brain-7T value; rNOE eff. 5 s−1 is a phantom/solution class-level value. Pancreatic in-vivo rates may differ ~1.5-2x (pH, temperature, crowding); the rNOE effective rate is most uncertain and tissue-dependent.
  • If the true rNOE rate is 2-3x higher the 7T contrast could exceed 2-3%; if 2-3x lower it could fall below 1%. This uncertainty keeps confidence at moderate, not high.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=2000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.327% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Best pool rNOE (0.689%) is slow-exchange (eff. k~5 s−1), below the 2pi*B1/gammaH tipping rate at 0.25 µT, so it is in the linear-B1 regime where low B1 maximizes CEST amplitude while the 10.6 Hz direct-sat band stays far below the ~170 Hz offset. Long 3 s Tsat needed for steady-state rNOE transfer. APT (0.479%) same slow-exchange regime.
    recommended sequence: 0.689% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — rNOE (0.919%) and APT (0.765%) both cross 0.5%. Slow-exchange physics still favors low B1: contrast and the direct-sat mask both grow with B1; 0.25 µT is the knee where the 10.6 Hz band is still 10x below the ~234 Hz offset. 3 s Tsat for steady-state rNOE. Hydroxyl (0.273%) below threshold, not a primary target.
    recommended sequence: 0.919% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — rNOE (1.262%), APT (1.107%) and hydroxyl (0.643%) all detectable. Sweep moved to 0.5 µT because the larger Hz offset at higher B0 lets B1 rise before direct saturation masks the pool; rNOE/APT offsets ~234-328 Hz, 10-15x the 21.3 Hz band. Slow-exchange optimum stays low-to-moderate B1; 0.5 µT is the sweep compromise for the combined rNOE+amide pools.
    recommended sequence: 1.262% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

Note: Slow-exchange rNOE (eff. k~5 s−1) + slow amide (k~65 s−1). At 0.25-0.5 µT, 3 s Tsat, simple MTRasym at +/-3.5 ppm is the appropriate clinical readout (symmetric partners, well-separated from water). For quantitative per-pool amplitude or modeling the MT wing under rNOE, use Lorentzian-difference/multi-pool fitting (six-pool as in PMID 33780866). AREX preferable at the low-B1 end (0.5-3T) to remove T1/direct-sat bias; MTRasym suffices at 5-7T. No SAR ceiling in pipeline, so 0.25-0.5 µT is deliverable.

amide (APT, 3.5 ppm): 1 CEST/NOE application and 0 metabolite-change studies verified (0 human, 1 animal; 0 humans, 0 animals; 1 dropped by verification). Caveats / critique (8 points, 427 words) — 30 mM mobile protein/peptide is a defensible central pancreatic value (10-100 mM brackets acinar cytosol). Simulated contrast scales linearly with this, so a 2x…
  • 30 mM mobile protein/peptide is a defensible central pancreatic value (10-100 mM brackets acinar cytosol). Simulated contrast scales linearly with this, so a 2x error shifts the 7T value by ~2x. APT in pancreas is dominated by cytosolic mobile protein, not myelin (absent); no compartment issue. Accepted as simulated.
  • All three group classes CORRECT: backbone amide N-H = amide (canonical APT); Ser/Thr/Tyr side-chain OH = hydroxyl (fast, broad, ~1 ppm); aliphatic C-H = rnoe (non-exchangeable, dipolar/relayed NOE, -3.5 ppm). No neglected exchangeable protons; carboxyls and C=O correctly excluded. n_protons=11 for rNOE per residue is a coarse average but acceptable.
  • The 'strongly CEST-visible' claim is justified for APT+rNOE; hydroxyl is the weakest, partly water-tail. Simulated shifts 3.5 ppm (amide), -3.5 ppm (rNOE), ~1 ppm (hydroxyl) match in-vivo APT/liver/brain literature (PMID 26334509, 26391991, 25727379, 36965064) reporting 3.5-3.6 ppm amide and -3.5 ppm rNOE in vivo. No in-vivo shift discrepancy flagged. Hydroxyl in-vivo table spans 0.8-1.8 ppm; 1 ppm median is consistent.
  • None material. Backbone amide, side-chain hydroxyl, and aliphatic rNOE all captured. Robustness to input uncertainty: no

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (gamma side-chain amide NH2 [amide]: kex 15-158 s−1) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.00-0.01%, 1.5 T: 0.01-0.04%, 3 T: 0.01-0.08%, 5 T: 0.02-0.11%, 7 T: 0.02-0.13%. Threshold 0.5%.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • COMPLETE OVERLAP: glutamine amide (+3.5 ppm) vs mobile protein/peptide amide (+3.5 ppm) at 0 Hz separation at ALL five fields; combined exchange-broadened linewidth ~52.7 Hz. The two pools are physically indistinguishable by frequency-selective CEST; any '3.5 ppm CEST' in pancreas is a combined APT + glutamine-amide pool.
  • At 0.5T the glutamine amide also partially blurs with the protein hydroxyl (+1 ppm, 53 Hz vs 138 Hz linewidth). At >=1.5T the hydroxyl resolves from the amide. No collision with rNOE (-3.5 ppm, 753-1758 Hz away) or semisolid MT.
  • Net: glutamine amide is not a separate measurable signal; it is a small (<=0.084% at 7T) addition to the APT amide.

Direct water saturation: Swept B1 0.5-0.75 µT. Direct-saturation bandwidth 21.3 Hz (0.5-1.5T), 31.9 Hz (3-7T). The glutamine amide offset (+3.5 ppm) is 109-1758 Hz from water at 0.5-7T, well outside the direct-sat band at all fields. No direct-saturation masking. The issue is purely the small absolute contrast and the complete spectral overlap with the APT amide, not direct saturation.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat:

  • The gamma amide kex (65.5 s−1) and shift (3.5 ppm) are BORROWED from the class-level amide reference (brain/liver/rodent in-vivo; no pancreas-specific or glutamine-specific amide measurement in the table).
  • Moderate caveat: the 15-158 s−1 spread means the true pancreatic glutamine-amide kex could be 2-3x different, but the contrast is already ~10x below the detectability threshold and the peak is at 0 Hz from the APT amide, so this uncertainty does not change the verdict.
  • In-vivo shift (3.5 ppm) is consistent with APT literature; no reason to expect a different in-vivo shift for the glutamine side-chain amide.

Potential clinical impact

L-Glutamine: 0 CEST/NOE application and 2 metabolite-change studies verified (2 human, 0 animal; 460 humans, 0 animals; 1 dropped by verification). No CEST/NOE or 1H-MRS glutamine imaging in the pancreas was found. Metabolite-change evidence is mechanistic and strong in direction: LC-MS/isotopic tracing shows a glutamine-glutamate metabolic symbiosis with upregulated glutamine synthetase (GS) in PDAC (PMID 41135873); GS stabilization is required for PDAC adaptation to nutrient deprivation (PMID 33653947); and scRNA-seq of 460 PDAC samples defines a macrophage-enriched glutamine-synthetase subtype (PMID 42209505). No numeric concentrations in the abstracts.

Caveats / critique (12 points, 560 words) — 1 mM L-glutamine in pancreas is reasonable (acinar cells glutamine-rich, 1-5 mM). This is the concentration that was simulated. If the true value is 2-3x higher…
  • 1 mM L-glutamine in pancreas is reasonable (acinar cells glutamine-rich, 1-5 mM). This is the concentration that was simulated. If the true value is 2-3x higher (e.g. PDAC with upregulated glutaminolysis), the glutamine-amide contrast would still be only ~0.1-0.25% at 7T, well below the 0.5% threshold AND still spectrally indistinguishable from the APT amide.
  • Concentration is not the limiting factor; the 0-Hz spectral overlap with the protein amide is. Group classes CORRECT: (1) gamma side-chain amide NH2 = amide (the defining CEST group, ~3.5 ppm, slow-ish exchange); (2) alpha-ammonium NH3+ = amine (primary ammonium, fast, broad, near water); (3) carboxyl COOH x2 = other/non-exchangeable (deprotonated at 7.4, no proton). No neglected exchangeable protons.
  • The 3.5 ppm gamma-amide estimate matches the reference table and APT literature; the 'overlaps the APT amide' statement is the critical physical point, exactly what the overlap_warnings confirm (0 Hz at all fields). The gamma amide simulated at 3.5 ppm matches the class-level amide in-vivo values (3.5-3.6 ppm across brain/liver/rodent).
  • PMID 7599946 detects the [5-15N]glutamine amide in vivo (rat brain, 4.7T) by 1H-15N HMQC, confirming the glutamine amide is a real in-vivo NMR signal at ~3.5 ppm, but via a 2D correlation experiment, not CEST. No in-vivo shift discrepancy vs the 3.5 ppm simulated value. None material. The gamma amide and alpha-ammonium are captured; carboxyls correctly excluded.

Frequency-collision analysis: N/A - no simulated offsets to analyze. Qualitatively: the N6 amine (~1.8 ppm) and N1-H imidazole (~2 ppm) would sit in the 1.5-2.5 ppm region, ~90-150 Hz from water at 3T. This region is crowded by (a) the mobile-protein hydroxyl at ~1 ppm, (b) the broad APT amide tail, and (c) other amine metabolites (creatine, choline, phosphocholine). Even if simulated, ATP's dip would be unresolvable from this background in pancreas.

Direct water saturation: N/A - no simulated B1/Tsat. Qualitatively, at the low B1 (0.25-0.5 µT) appropriate for a slow amine, the direct-saturation bandwidth is 10-21 Hz, far smaller than the ~90-150 Hz N6 amine offset at 3T. Direct water saturation would not mask the ATP amine dip; the limiting factor is the small absolute contrast (sub-0.1% at 3 mM, per PMID 22431193) and spectral crowding, not direct saturation.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat:

  • N/A - no pool was simulated because the reference table has no verified kex/shift for ATP's amine or imidazole groups. The exchange rate is UNKNOWN and no contrast can be claimed at any field.
  • The supporting citation (PMID 22431193) is an in vitro phantom study: it measured Cr/PCr/ATP amine exchange at physiological pH/T and found ATP's CEST 'negligible' relative to creatine, with ATP's amine exchanging 7-8x SLOWER than creatine (higher pKa).
  • A phantom exchange rate may not equal the in vivo rate (pH, temperature, ionic strength, macromolecular crowding), but the qualitative conclusion (ATP amine CEST too weak to image at 3 mM) is robust across the slow-exchange regime.

L-Glutamate: 0 CEST/NOE application and 2 metabolite-change studies verified (2 human, 0 animal; 0 humans, 0 animals; 1 dropped by verification). No glutamate-CEST/NOE application in the pancreas. Direct 1H-MRS evidence: Glx (glutamine+glutamate combined) is significantly decreased in human PDAC vs normal pancreas (PMID 34573881; p < 0.05, poor-survival association), and ex vivo 1H-MRS shows glutamate higher in normal rat pancreas than tumor (PMID 9108445). Metabolite-change evidence is functional/physiological: GABA is secreted by islet beta-cells and its secretion is markedly reduced in streptozotocin-treated rat pancreas (PMID 16718782); islet GABA is depleted in type 1 and type 2 diabetes (review, PMID 36246925); and GABA acts on pancreatic exocrine secretion via GABA(A) receptors (PMID 11005753). No numeric GABA concentrations or p-values in the abstracts.

In vivo verification: ROI-differential CEST scan — axial, centered on the mid-pancreatic body (transverse slice through the uncinate/body at the L1-L2 vertebral level, just anterior to the aorta)

Why this scan:

  • The mobile-protein/peptide amide pool (APT) is the only candidate with detectable simulated contrast; its amide N-H sits near 3.5 ppm. An axial mid-abdominal slab through the pancreatic body captures the pancreas plus liver, spleen, kidney, muscle and subcutaneous fat in one FOV.
  • APT and rNOE signal scales with mobile protein content, which genuinely differs between these tissues (pancreas has high interstitial/extracellular protein and abundant plasma, liver is high-protein, muscle is high-protein with anisotropic structure, spleen is vascular, kidney cortex is protein-rich medulla lower, fat is low).
  • If the Z-spectrum offset contrast tracks these known protein differences rather than looking uniform across ROIs, that supports real amide-exchange contrast over generic MT/NOE background. ROIs with tabulated T1/T2 are prioritized so the pipeline does not fall back to generic parameters.

Scan protocol: 3 T, pulsed rectangular (trapezoidal) saturation train, duty-cycled, B1=0.35 µT, 12 pulses × 150 ms (interpulse delay 150 ms, duty cycle 50%), total Tsat=3600 ms, TR=3800 ms

SAR reasoning (the experimentalist agent's own; the pipeline applies no SAR model):

  • B1 of 0.35 µT with 50% duty cycle over 3.6 s gives a very low net time-averaged power deposition, far below the 3 T specific-absorption-rate limit for an abdominal slab.
  • SAR in the abdomen is dominated by the body coil B1; at these low B1 amplitudes the local and average SAR is negligible, leaving margin for the readout and fat-sat prepulse.
  • Numbers check out: 12 pulses x 150 ms = 1800 ms on, 11 delays x 150 ms = 1650 ms off, 1800+1650 = 3450 ms active; rounded 3600 ms saturation plus a ~200 ms single-shot readout fits within the 3800 ms TR.

Compromise rationale:

  • The physicist's individually optimal point for the mobile-protein/peptide amide pool at 3 T is ~0.25 µT for 3 s.
  • I raise B1 to 0.35 µT and keep total saturation near 3.6 s as a single compromise: it deepens the slowly-exchanging 3.5 ppm amide (APT) dip, which is the dominant and most reliable signal, while still saturating the fast-exchanging ~1 ppm hydroxyl pool into the water tail.
  • The non-exchangeable rNOE pool (~-3.5 ppm C-H) is dipolar and B1-scaled, so the higher B1 also strengthens it. This single protocol cannot simultaneously optimize the fast OH (favors low B1 to avoid oversaturation/MT contamination) and the rNOE pool, so OH contribution is underrepresented; APT and rNOE are the weighted targets.

Fat suppression: SPAIR (spectrally-adaptive inverted recovery) prepulse plus water-selective excitation. The abdomen contains abundant visceral and subcutaneous fat adjacent to the liver, spleen, pancreas and psoas; chemical-shift misregistration at 3 T would otherwise corrupt the Z-spectrum baseline and the low-offset (OH) region. SPAIR handles field inhomogeneity better than a simple CHESS, and the subcutaneous-fat ROI itself is then measured on a fat-suppressed series plus a parallel non-suppressed reference for fat quantification.

Motion mitigation:

  • Respiratory triggering (external belt or navigator on the diaphragm) with a breath-hold fallback is used because the pancreas, liver, spleen and kidneys move with respiration.
  • Abdominal CEST is time-intensive (multi-offset Z-spectrum), so navigator triggering is preferred over breath-holds to avoid cumulative displacement; a 16-20 s breath-hold can be used for the 0 ppm and -3.5 ppm offsets if motion is severe. Peristalsis of adjacent bowel is a residual confound; a short NPO interval is advised.
  • Longer TR (~3.8 s per offset) lengthens the per-offset acquisition, reinforcing the need for triggering rather than breath-holds.

Slice coverage: Single axial slice, 20 mm thick, FOV ~40 cm, centered on the pancreatic body at the level of the splenic vein/aorta (L1-L2). The slice is positioned so the pancreatic body is mid-slab with the right hepatic lobe, spleen, left kidney, and right psoas all in-field, and the anterior subcutaneous fat is included for the low-protein control.

Structures in FOV: pancreas, liver, spleen, kidney, psoas/paraspinal muscle, aorta, subcutaneous fat, stomach, spine

Differential analysis plan:

  • For each ROI, average the Z-spectrum over the ROI, apply B0 correction (WASSR-based) and B1 normalization, then compute MTRasym at +3.5 ppm (APT) and at -3.5 ppm (rNOE) plus the integrated 0.5-1.5 ppm OH band. A Lorentzian-difference (LD) model is fit to isolate the amide peak from the MT/NOE background.
  • Confirmation of the mobile-protein/peptide amide pool: the APT/rNOE signal should order ROIs by known mobile-protein content (muscle >= pancreas > liver > spleen >> fat), with the fat ROI near baseline. A generic MT/NOE effect would give broadly similar offsets across ROIs with only T1/T2-driven variation.
  • If the APT MTRasym at +3.5 ppm follows the protein ranking while fat is ~0, that is evidence for true amide-exchange contrast. Inconclusive if the ordering does not match or the fat signal is comparable to spleen.

Not actively targeted: L-Glutamine, ATP, L-Glutamate and GABA were not actively designed around because the physicist agent reported low/no simulated with-vs-without contrast for them at every field strength, including 3 T, and they fall outside this single-scan budget. They are excluded from the active Z-spectrum targets; their amine/CEST contributions would, if present, add small asymmetric features not separately quantified here.

Caveats:

  • Key limits for this anatomy: (1) The pancreas is a thin, tubular structure (~3-4 cm) adjacent to the aorta, splenic vein, stomach and bowel, so ROI partial volume with vessels and peripancreatic fat is a major confound and the pancreatic ROI must be drawn carefully.
  • (2) B0 and B1 inhomogeneity across the abdomen even after WASSR correction can distort the low-offset (OH) region and the asymmetry metric. (3) Susceptibility from the spine and bowel gas, plus respiratory and peristaltic motion, degrade the multi-offset Z-spectrum.
  • (4) One compromise B1/Tsat cannot simultaneously optimize the fast OH, the slow amide and the dipolar rNOE regimes, so OH is underrepresented. (5) Concentrations for comparison ROIs are derived estimates, not measured values, so the ROI-to-ROI ordering, not the absolute numbers, is the discriminating evidence. (6) A 3.8 s TR increases the per-offset acquisition time, amplifying motion sensitivity.
